name: Learn: Ingress TLS
objective: CKS › Cluster Setup (10%). Goal: terminate TLS at the Ingress with a Kubernetes TLS Secret — generate a self-signed cert, store it as a kubernetes.io/tls Secret, reference it from an Ingress tls block for a host, verify host-to-backend routing, keep TLS and rule hosts aligned, and rotate the cert in place.
description: Master TLS termination at the Ingress step by step — create a kubernetes.io/tls Secret from a self-signed cert, wire an Ingress tls block to it for a host, confirm the host routes to the backing Service, keep the tls host aligned with the rule host, and rotate the certificate in place.

questions.title: Create a kubernetes.io/tls Secret
questions.teach:
An Ingress terminates HTTPS by reading a certificate + private key from a **Secret of type `kubernetes.io/tls`**. That special type requires exactly two keys: **`tls.crt`** (the PEM certificate) and **`tls.key`** (the PEM private key). The API validates the pair on create (the key must match the cert).

For learning you generate a **self-signed** cert with `openssl` (CKS exams and real clusters usually feed you a CA-issued one, or cert-manager provisions it, but the Secret shape is identical). The fast path is `kubectl create secret tls <name> --cert=<file> --key=<file>` — it sets `type: kubernetes.io/tls` and both keys for you.

**Secret types you should know (CKS):**
- `generic` (aka `Opaque`) — arbitrary key/value, e.g. `--from-literal`, `--from-file`.
- `kubernetes.io/tls` — exactly `tls.crt` + `tls.key`; used by Ingress.
- `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` — registry pull creds (`--docker-server/...`).

**Three ways a pod/controller consumes a Secret (symmetric with ConfigMaps — swap `secret*`→`configMap*`):**
- single-key env via `valueFrom.secretKeyRef`;
- bulk env via `envFrom.secretRef`;
- **volume mount** — each key becomes a file (use `subPath` to mount one key as a single file). Ingress uses the Secret internally; the controller reads it by name — you do not mount it.

**Gotchas:**
- Data in a Secret is **base64-encoded**, not encrypted (unless EncryptionConfiguration is enabled at the API server — a CKS topic). `kubectl create secret tls` handles the encoding for you.
- env values are **read once at pod start**; a changed Secret does NOT update a running container's env, but a **mounted** Secret does update (eventually). Ingress controllers watch the Secret and reload the cert on change.
- `immutable: true` locks a Secret (faster, but then you can only delete+recreate).
- The `secretName` referenced by an Ingress must live in the **same namespace** as the Ingress.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `ingress-learn`, generate a self-signed cert + key on the host for CN `demo.example.com`, then create a TLS Secret named `web-tls` from them.

Target: Secret `web-tls` is type `kubernetes.io/tls` and has both `tls.crt` and `tls.key`.
questions.hint: `openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com"`, then `kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key`.
questions.solution:
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com"
kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}'   # kubernetes.io/tls

verification.description: Secret web-tls is type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt and tls.key

questions.title: Add a tls block to an Ingress
questions.teach:
An Ingress enables HTTPS via **`spec.tls`**, a list where each entry names a **`secretName`** (the `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret) and the **`hosts`** it covers. When a request arrives for one of those hosts, the controller presents that Secret's certificate and terminates TLS at the edge (the connection to the backend Service is typically plain HTTP).

**Ingress fields to know (CKS/CKAD):**
- `ingressClassName` — picks which controller handles this Ingress (replaces the old `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation). Without a running controller + a class, nothing is actually served.
- `spec.rules[].host` + `.http.paths[]` — each path has a `pathType` (**`Prefix`**, **`Exact`**, or `ImplementationSpecific`) and a `backend.service` (name + port).
- `spec.defaultBackend` — catch-all for unmatched requests.
- `spec.tls[]` — one or more `{hosts: [...], secretName: ...}` entries. Omit `hosts` and the controller may use the Secret's cert as a default.

**Gotchas:**
- The `secretName` Secret must be in the **same namespace** as the Ingress and be type `kubernetes.io/tls`.
- `spec.tls.hosts` must match the hostnames in `spec.rules` — a mismatch means that host is served over plain HTTP with no cert (you harden this in a later step).
- TLS at the Ingress is **termination** only; it does not require (or create) HTTPS to the pod.
- An Ingress does nothing without an **ingress controller** installed and selected by `ingressClassName`; `kubectl apply` succeeds regardless.
- SNI: controllers pick the cert by the request's host (Server Name Indication); a wildcard cert (`*.example.com`) can cover `hosts: ['*.example.com']`.
questions.prompt:
A Deployment `web` and Service `web` (port 80) are already running in `ingress-learn`. Create an Ingress named `web` with a `tls` block referencing Secret `web-tls` for host `demo.example.com`.

Target: Ingress `web` has a `spec.tls` entry whose `secretName` is `web-tls` and whose `hosts` includes `demo.example.com`.
questions.hint: In the Ingress YAML add `spec.tls: [{hosts: [demo.example.com], secretName: web-tls}]`. You can author the full Ingress (rules + tls) in one manifest and `kubectl apply -f`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: ingress-learn
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - demo.example.com
    secretName: web-tls
  rules:
  - host: demo.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

verification.description: Ingress web spec.tls references secretName web-tls for host demo.example.com

questions.title: Route the host to the backend Service
questions.teach:
TLS only matters if traffic actually reaches your app. An Ingress **rule** maps a **`host`** to one or more HTTP paths, each with a **`backend.service`** (name + port). Terminating TLS for `demo.example.com` but never routing it to the `web` Service would leave HTTPS clients with nowhere to go.

**Path matching (`pathType`):**
- **`Prefix`** — matches by URL path segments (`/` matches everything under it). Most common.
- **`Exact`** — matches the path exactly (case-sensitive, no trailing-slash fuzz).
- `ImplementationSpecific` — delegated to the controller (behavior varies; avoid in exams unless asked).

**Backend targets a Service, which has its own type:**
- `backend.service.port` can be a **`number`** (e.g. 80) OR a **`name`** (the Service's named port) — not both.
- The Service behind an Ingress is almost always **`ClusterIP`** (the Ingress is the external entry point; you don't need NodePort/LoadBalancer on the Service itself).
- `backend.resource` is an alternative to `backend.service` for referencing a custom resource (rare).

**Gotchas:**
- The referenced **Service must exist** and have endpoints (healthy pods) — a dangling backend yields 502/503 from the controller.
- Port must match what the Service actually exposes (`service.port`), not the container's `targetPort`.
- `defaultBackend` (if set) catches requests that match no rule/host; otherwise the controller returns its default 404.
- Make sure the rule for `demo.example.com` has a path whose backend is Service `web` on port `80` — the same Service your cert is protecting.
questions.prompt:
Confirm (and fix if needed) that Ingress `web` routes host `demo.example.com` to Service `web` on port `80`.

Target: a rule with `host: demo.example.com` has a path whose `backend.service.name` is `web` and port `80`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o yaml` and check `spec.rules[*].host` and `spec.rules[*].http.paths[*].backend.service`. If it is missing, re-apply the Ingress from step 2 which includes the rule.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o yaml
# rule host demo.example.com -> service web:80 (apply the step-2 manifest if absent)

verification.description: Ingress rule host demo.example.com routes to service web port 80

questions.title: Keep the tls host aligned with the rule host
questions.teach:
A common misconfiguration: the `spec.tls` `hosts` list does not match the `spec.rules` `host`. The controller then serves the rule's host over plain HTTP (no cert matched) instead of terminating TLS — effectively leaving the app reachable without HTTPS. From a hardening standpoint every routed host should have a matching tls entry so nothing is served unencrypted by accident.

The fix is simple: ensure **every host in `spec.rules` also appears in some `spec.tls.hosts`** entry. For this Ingress that means `demo.example.com` must be in both.

**Host-matching rules to remember:**
- Hostnames are matched **exactly** or via a **wildcard** (`*.example.com` matches `a.example.com` but NOT the bare `example.com` and NOT `a.b.example.com` — exactly one label).
- A rule with **no `host`** matches all inbound hosts; a `tls` entry with **no `hosts`** can act as a default cert. Mixing these loosely is how plain-HTTP leaks happen.
- TLS SNI selection is by host, so the cert's CN/SAN should also cover the host — otherwise clients get a name-mismatch warning even though the controller terminates TLS.

**Hardening / redirect gotchas:**
- Many controllers (e.g. ingress-nginx) serve the host on **both** 80 and 443 unless you force a redirect (annotation `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"`, on by default when a tls block exists for that host). No tls entry = no redirect = plain HTTP stays open.
- A host listed under `rules` but absent from any `tls.hosts` is the classic "served unencrypted by accident" bug this step checks.
questions.prompt:
Harden Ingress `web`: ensure every host it routes also has TLS, i.e. the `spec.tls` hosts cover the `spec.rules` host with no mismatch.

Target: the set of hosts under `spec.rules` is fully covered by `spec.tls[*].hosts` (every rule host appears in tls hosts).
questions.hint: Compare `kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[*].host}'` with `{.spec.tls[*].hosts[*]}`. They must match for demo.example.com. Re-apply a corrected manifest if a host is only in rules.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[*].host}{"\n"}{.spec.tls[*].hosts[*]}{"\n"}'
# both must list demo.example.com; fix the manifest so every rule host is in a tls hosts list

verification.description: every spec.rules host is covered by a spec.tls hosts entry (no plain-HTTP-only host)

questions.title: Rotate the certificate in place
questions.teach:
Certificates expire or get compromised, so you must be able to **rotate** them. Because the Ingress references the Secret **by name**, you can swap the certificate without touching the Ingress at all: generate a fresh cert+key and replace the Secret's contents under the **same name**. The Ingress keeps pointing at `web-tls` and the controller picks up the new cert.

**Ways to replace a Secret in place:**
- **Apply from dry-run (recommended):** `kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -` — idempotent, works whether or not it exists.
- **Delete + recreate:** `kubectl delete secret web-tls` then `kubectl create secret tls web-tls ...` — simple, but leaves a brief window with no cert.
- **`kubectl replace`:** needs the full object and the Secret to already exist.
- **`kubectl edit`:** only practical if you hand-base64 the new `tls.crt`/`tls.key` — error-prone, avoid for certs.

**Gotchas:**
- `kubectl apply` on a Secret you originally made with `create` can warn about a **missing last-applied-configuration annotation** — the dry-run-then-apply pattern avoids that and is the clean idiom.
- If the Secret is **`immutable: true`**, you cannot update it at all — you must delete and recreate.
- Controllers watch the Secret and **hot-reload** the new cert (no Ingress edit, no pod restart) — that is the zero-downtime point. The reload is near-instant but not strictly atomic for in-flight TLS handshakes.
- Do **not** edit the Ingress during rotation — it references by name; changing the name would break the link.
- After rotation, confirm the Secret is still type `kubernetes.io/tls` with both keys and the Ingress still references it.
questions.prompt:
Rotate `web-tls`: generate a new self-signed cert+key for `demo.example.com` and replace the Secret (same name `web-tls`), keeping the Ingress reference intact.

Target: Secret `web-tls` still exists, is type `kubernetes.io/tls` with tls.crt+tls.key, and Ingress `web` still references it in spec.tls.
questions.hint: Regenerate with openssl, then `kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -`. Don't edit the Ingress — it references by name.
questions.solution:
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com"
kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls[*].secretName}'   # web-tls

verification.description: web-tls rotated (still kubernetes.io/tls) and Ingress web still references it
